section: COLD OPEN (0:00–0:50)
text: On November thirteenth, we stood on a beach across the water from Starbase, Texas, and watched the most powerful rocket ever built leave the ground.

section: COLD OPEN (0:00–0:50)
text: A few minutes later, SpaceX called off the booster catch. We watched it come down in a fireball.

section: COLD OPEN (0:00–0:50)
text: Twenty-two and a half hours and fourteen orbits later, the Ship came home, and the tower's giant arms caught it. The first time SpaceX has ever done that.

section: COLD OPEN (0:00–0:50)
text: But the biggest story here isn't happening in the sky. It's happening on the ground. In land deals, highways, water plants, and tax breaks. And it's reshaping the Rio Grande Valley.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: Starbase sits at the very southern tip of Texas, on Boca Chica, about twenty miles east of Brownsville. A decade ago, this was a handful of beach houses at the end of a two-lane road.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: Today it's a company town. SpaceX's workforce here grew from about three hundred people in twenty twenty to more than thirty-four hundred by twenty twenty-four. And it isn't slowing down.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: Why does catching a rocket matter to the Valley? Because catching and reusing rockets is how SpaceX plans to launch far more often. More launches means more building, more hiring, and more traffic down that one road to Boca Chica.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: Two projects are driving the next wave. The first is called GigaBay: a seven-hundred-thousand-square-foot factory, a five-hundred-and-six-million-dollar investment, built to produce Starship rockets at a pace SpaceX describes as a thousand per year.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: The second is a four-hundred-and-eighty-million-dollar expansion of launch infrastructure, including two launch pads, so SpaceX can fly more often.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: Each project is expected to bring about five hundred jobs, and SpaceX says at least a quarter of those positions will go to local hires.

section: PART 1 — WHAT'S BEING BUILT (0:50–3:00)
text: For a region that's long been one of the poorest in Texas, that's a big deal. For anyone who builds or invests here, the question is simple: where are those thousand-plus workers going to live?

section: PART 1B — THE HOUSING QUESTION (3:00–4:45)
text: Start with Brownsville, the city of about a hundred and eighty-eight thousand people that sits between Starbase and the rest of the Valley.

section: PART 1B — THE HOUSING QUESTION (3:00–4:45)
text: According to Census survey data, the median home in Brownsville is valued at about a hundred and twenty-two thousand dollars. The Texas median is about two hundred and sixty thousand. That's less than half.

section: PART 1B — THE HOUSING QUESTION (3:00–4:45)
text: Incomes are lower too. Brownsville's median household income is about forty-nine thousand dollars a year, compared with about seventy-six thousand statewide.

section: PART 1B — THE HOUSING QUESTION (3:00–4:45)
text: For builders, that gap cuts both ways. Low land and home prices are exactly what makes new projects pencil out here. But if thousands of higher-paying aerospace jobs keep arriving, watch for pressure on rents and entry-level homes, especially on the east side of Brownsville along Highway 4, and in the communities closest to Starbase across the water.

section: PART 1B — THE HOUSING QUESTION (3:00–4:45)
text: That's the opportunity in one sentence: a fast-growing employer, in one of the most affordable housing markets in Texas. The question is whether the roads, the water, and the zoning can keep up.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: Everything at Starbase depends on one road: State Highway 4, the two-lane highway from Brownsville to Boca Chica.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: Texas plans to spend more than a hundred and ninety-two million dollars to widen about fourteen miles of it into a four-lane divided highway, rebuilt in concrete to handle heavy trucks. TxDOT says crash rates on this stretch run one and a half to two times the state average.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: But here's the timeline that matters for developers: construction bids aren't expected until the fall of twenty twenty-seven, and the work could take two and a half to three years. So the road that everything depends on won't be finished until around twenty thirty.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: Then there's water. In August, Brownsville's city commission held a six-hour Saturday meeting and voted unanimously to remove about four hundred and forty-five acres near the Port of Brownsville from the city limits, at SpaceX's request.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: In exchange, SpaceX agreed to pay the city up to two hundred and twenty million dollars for water projects. Forty million up front, then six quarterly payments of thirty million.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: That money pays for two projects: a wastewater reclamation plant adding about eight million gallons a day, and a water plant expansion adding about ten million more. Brownsville uses about twenty-one million gallons a day today, and seventy percent of that comes from the Rio Grande.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: And the river is under strain. Upstream, Falcon and Amistad reservoirs have run low in recent years. Under the 1944 water treaty, Mexico owes the United States one point seven five million acre-feet of water every five years. When the last cycle closed in October twenty twenty-five, Texas officials said Mexico fell short.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: That's why the mayor's comment matters. He says the SpaceX deal could reduce, or even eliminate, the city's reliance on the Rio Grande. In a region where water is the quiet limit on growth, that's a major opportunity.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: And Brownsville isn't the only place investing. Across the Lower Valley, a proposed one-hundred-and-sixty-four-million-dollar package from the North American Development Bank and the Texas Water Development Board would line and pipe old irrigation canals, so less water is lost before it ever reaches a farm or a faucet. Those approvals are still pending.

section: PART 2 — THE ROAD AND THE WATER (4:45–8:00)
text: But there was a catch. SpaceX said the offer was only good if the commission voted that same day. Residents asked why the city was rushing, and what SpaceX planned to do with the land. Even the mayor admitted, quote, "It is rushed. There's no doubt."

section: PART 3 — THE BIGGER PICTURE, AND THE RISKS (8:00–10:15)
text: Now zoom out. SpaceX's biggest Texas announcement this year wasn't in the Valley at all. In Grimes County, northwest of Houston, the governor's office announced a chip plant SpaceX calls Terafab: more than sixteen point eight billion dollars in its first phase, with three thousand jobs.

section: PART 3 — THE BIGGER PICTURE, AND THE RISKS (8:00–10:15)
text: And in August, SpaceX announced a hundred-billion-dollar launch site in Louisiana. Starbase is still the heart of Starship. But SpaceX now has options, and options mean leverage.

section: PART 3 — THE BIGGER PICTURE, AND THE RISKS (8:00–10:15)
text: You heard that leverage in Brownsville: take the deal today, or we'll look at our other facilities.

section: PART 3 — THE BIGGER PICTURE, AND THE RISKS (8:00–10:15)
text: There are other questions too. Starbase is a city whose three-member commission includes two SpaceX employees, and it nominated SpaceX for up to seven and a half million dollars in state tax refunds, through a program meant for economically distressed areas. Critics, like the watchdog group Good Jobs First, ask whether a company worth hundreds of billions of dollars needs that help.

section: PART 3 — THE BIGGER PICTURE, AND THE RISKS (8:00–10:15)
text: And then there's the nature of the business itself. This is a test program. In two days, we saw a booster lost and a ship caught. Setbacks can bring investigations and pauses, and launch schedules can shift. If you're betting on Starbase's growth, you're betting on a company still learning to fly.

section: PART 4 — WHAT IT MEANS FOR BUILDERS AND INVESTORS (10:15–11:30)
text: So what does this mean if you build, buy, or lend in the Valley?

section: PART 4 — WHAT IT MEANS FOR BUILDERS AND INVESTORS (10:15–11:30)
text: On the opportunity side: a thousand-plus new jobs need places to live, in a market where homes cost less than half the state median. Brownsville and the communities closest to Starbase are first in line for workforce housing demand. Suppliers, contractors, and industrial users follow big factories. And new water capacity, if it gets built, is what lets new subdivisions get permitted.

section: PART 4 — WHAT IT MEANS FOR BUILDERS AND INVESTORS (10:15–11:30)
text: On the risk side: much of this depends on one company. The road won't be wider until around twenty thirty. The water projects depend on SpaceX's payments arriving on schedule. And SpaceX is spreading its bets across Texas and beyond.

section: PART 4 — WHAT IT MEANS FOR BUILDERS AND INVESTORS (10:15–11:30)
text: Before you underwrite a project here, ask three questions. How much of your demand depends on Starbase? What's the water and road timeline for your site? And what happens to your numbers if launch schedules slip a year?

Starbase just pulled off a first in spaceflight. Whether it becomes a first for the Valley's economy depends on what gets built on the ground. We'll keep tracking it. Sources are in the description. This is RGV News.
